title: Knowledge Check 3: Lessons 11-15
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 11-15 of the ai-adoption series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: An employee passes the training assessment but still works the old way weeks later. What does this show?
options: A motivation problem that stricter mandates and reminders would correct
The transfer gap: learning happened but did not reach daily work
A flawed assessment that let the wrong person pass
A workload problem that more sessions would solve
questions.explanation: Transfer requires applying the skill beyond the training example and keeping it after the session ends. Passing an assessment proves learning, not that the behavior survived the return to work.

questions.question: Why does one intensive workshop produce weaker long-term retention than short sessions repeated over several weeks?
options: Short sessions cover less content, so each piece is easier to absorb
Workshops create pressure that blocks people from learning the material
Spacing repetitions over time builds stronger memory than massing them
Repeated sessions are easier to fit around busy working weeks
questions.explanation: Spaced practice beats massed practice because each repetition lands after some forgetting has occurred. A single sitting feels efficient, but retention fades once people leave the room.

questions.question: A program needs training to keep serving new hires without the adoption owner running every session. Which structure does that?
options: Reusable material delivered by local champions on a repeating cadence
The owner running more sessions each quarter as headcount grows
New hires watching a recording of the original launch workshop
Requiring the launch module to be finished within the first working week
questions.explanation: Material is written once, delivery passes to champions who know the local work, and the reinforcement cadence runs without the owner. That division of labor is what lets training scale with headcount.

questions.question: A user abandons a tool after one wrong answer despite months of good results. What pattern is this?
options: Algorithm aversion, where one visible error outweighs a strong record
Sound risk management, since a single error proves the tool is unreliable
A training gap, since the user never learned the tool's limits
Ordinary churn that no intervention can reasonably influence
questions.explanation: People lose confidence in an automated tool faster than in a person after seeing the same mistake, even when the tool has performed better. The reaction follows the visible failure, not the track record.

questions.question: Which preparation most reduces the chance a user quits after a first bad output?
options: Waiting for the first failure to happen and then apologizing every time it does
Presenting only the tool's strengths so initial confidence stays high
Requiring users to accept the output without any independent check
Stating up front what the tool does well, where it invents, and how to check
questions.explanation: Most bad first experiences come from a wrong expectation rather than a broken tool. Naming the weak range and the quick check in advance turns a bad answer into a risk the user already knows how to manage.

questions.question: After a bad output, why should the explanation come before a low-stakes retry?
options: The explanation replaces any need for further use of the tool
The explanation gives the error a shape, and the retry rebuilds trust
The retry works only if the user first accepts that the tool is basically reliable
The order does not matter as long as both steps happen eventually
questions.explanation: An explanation converts a mystery into a navigable event, so the user knows the shape of the error. The retry then adds a small checkable win while the user stays in control of the output.

questions.question: Surveys say most staff use the new tool weekly, but usage logs show most rarely touch it. What explains the gap?
options: Usage logs are usually wrong because they miss work that happens offline
People report what they believe is expected, so stated use leads actual use
Staff are deliberately misreporting usage and should be held accountable for it
The survey sample must have been far too small to mean anything
questions.explanation: Self-reports drift toward the answer the organization wants to hear, so stated use runs ahead of enacted use. Behavior records collected as a byproduct of the work are the more honest evidence.

questions.question: A team collects detailed usage data for a quarter and changes nothing. What is missing?
options: A larger and more representative sample gathered before conclusions
A clearer dashboard that presents the same usage data in a more compelling way
The close: a visible change from the signals, with people told what changed
More frequent surveys to confirm what the usage data already shows
questions.explanation: Collecting signals without acting on them is data hoarding, and people stop supplying signal when nothing changes. The visible change plus telling people what it was and why keeps the loop alive.

questions.question: Which signal most directly shows that an approved tool does not fit the job?
options: People quietly routing around it with their own tools or the old way
People saying in a review meeting that the tool is working well
A high completion rate on the tool's onboarding module
A rising number of questions asked about how the tool is supposed to work
questions.explanation: A workaround is the clearest evidence that the approved tool does not match the work, because it is an action rather than an opinion. Reports of satisfaction can be shaped by what people think leadership wants to hear.

questions.question: Why does requiring a human check on every output weaken supervision?
options: It slows the workflow enough that people stop using the tool
Attention flattens, so the outputs that matter get the same glance
It removes the reviewer's authority to reject an output they disagree with
It conflicts with the vendor's terms for enterprise deployments
questions.explanation: People cannot sustain attention across a stream of items they mostly do not need to care about. A blanket check turns review into ritual, so the few outputs that need real judgment get no more scrutiny than the rest.

questions.question: Final pricing is sent to a customer and cannot be taken back once issued. Which oversight model fits?
options: Human-on-the-loop, with a supervisor watching for anomalies
Human-in-command only, with no review of individual outputs
No human review, because the system's accuracy record is strong
Human-in-the-loop, with a named person approving before release
questions.explanation: The bar is set by consequence and reversibility, so high stakes and hard-to-undo work needs a named sign-off before it leaves. Watching from above suits routine work where catching an occasional anomaly is enough.

questions.question: A reviewer approves every output in seconds without reading it. Which failure is this, and what corrects it?
options: Scattered oversight, which a stricter blanket rule would correct
Automation bias, which a defect prompt asking what is wrong corrects
A capability gap, which more training on the tool would close
A capacity problem, which adding more reviewers to the queue would solve
questions.explanation: When output is usually right, reviewers stop looking, which is automation bias. Asking what is specifically wrong forces a real read, and a rubber-stamper cannot name a defect.

questions.question: Under the color rule, what should an employee do with material that includes customer records?
options: Paste it into any tool after removing the customer's name
Paste it into an approved tool, since approval covers every data type
Keep it out of any public or unapproved tool, with no exceptions
Paste a full export so the tool has complete context to work from
questions.explanation: Records that would cause real damage if they left the building sit in the non-negotiable tier and never enter an unvetted tool. Removing a name does not make that material safe.

questions.question: Which gap most reliably turns an AI policy into a document nobody follows?
options: It is written in a formal legal register that most staff skim past and never apply
It omits a tool that the company has not adopted yet
It runs longer than a single page of plain and readable text
No owner keeps it current, answers questions, or handles violations
questions.explanation: A policy without a named owner lives in a folder, gets signed once, and is forgotten, so nobody can answer whether something is allowed. Ownership is what keeps the document current enough to mean anything.

questions.question: An employee wants a tool that is not on the approved list. Which part of the policy tells them what to do?
options: The data handling rule, which classifies the tool's risk
The change process, which gives a review path and a decision
The acknowledgment step, which records that they read the policy
The prohibited list, which names uses that are off limits
questions.explanation: An approved list stays current only when a defined request path sits behind it. Without that path people either hide their tools or adopt them while the policy falls behind reality.
